Package org.aeonbits.owner.handlers

Class AesGcmHandler

java.lang.Object
org.aeonbits.owner.handlers.AesGcmHandler
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, ValueHandler
public class AesGcmHandler extends Object implements ValueHandler
The cipher this library ships: AES-256/GCM over a passphrase, behind the name aes-gcm. 
     ConfigFactory.registerValueHandler(new AesGcmHandler(passphrase));
 
     db.password = ${$aes-gcm::AAM0IHNhbHQ...}

The passphrase never comes from the properties, which would be circular. It arrives here, from wherever the application already keeps it, and the configuration is created afterwards.

The token

     base64( iterations(4) | salt(16) | iv(12) | ciphertext | tag(16) )

Everything decryption depends on travels with the value, and the first 32 bytes are passed to GCM as additional authenticated data, so the header is covered by the tag and cannot be edited on its own. Base64 is the standard alphabet with padding: + / = all survive inside ${...}, and the one character a payload may not contain - } - base64 never produces.

Why the iteration count is in the token. It is an output and not a knob: the tool writes it, no syntax offers it to whoever edits the file, and a token that carries one below MINIMUM_ITERATIONS is refused rather than honoured, so it cannot be used to weaken anything. What it buys is that raising DEFAULT_ITERATIONS as guidance moves never orphans a file already written - which is the whole cost a fixed count would have had, since a token gives the reader nothing to derive with otherwise.

What the construction is for

  • A random IV per value, so that two equal secrets do not produce equal cipher text. This is what the AES/ECB example this library used to publish got wrong, and it is visible from outside: a file discloses which of its secrets are the same.
  • GCM, so that an edited value fails loudly instead of decrypting to something else.
  • PBKDF2 over a passphrase of any length, which is what removes the padding-to-16-characters the old example forced on a key.

Deriving once, not per value

A per-value salt would mean a per-value key derivation, and at 210,000 iterations ten encrypted properties would be ten derivations every time a configuration is created. The way out is not a weaker salt: the encrypting tool uses one random salt per invocation, so the values it writes in one run share it, and this class caches the derived key by salt and count. A salt shared by the values of one file is still unique to that file and that deployment, which is what a salt is for, while the IV stays per value, which is what stops equal secrets looking equal.

Rotation

A handler is registered under a name, so two of them can be registered at once: 

     ConfigFactory.registerValueHandler(new AesGcmHandler("aes-gcm-2025", current));
     ConfigFactory.registerValueHandler(new AesGcmHandler("aes-gcm-2024", previous));

and a rotation becomes an edit to the file, one value at a time, with both keys readable meanwhile.

Serialization

A Config object is serializable, and this handler is reachable from one. The passphrase and the derived keys are transient: writing them out would put a secret on disk in a file nobody chose to protect. A handler that comes back from deserialization therefore cannot decrypt, and says so.

    • DEFAULT_ITERATIONS

      public static final int DEFAULT_ITERATIONS
      What a value is encrypted with today: OWASP's current guidance for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256.

      Measured before being chosen, since the Java 8 baseline is the case that had to survive it: one derivation at this count costs 38 ms on JDK 24 and 49 ms on JDK 17, and it happens once per salt - which is once per file, not once per value.

      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • MINIMUM_ITERATIONS

      public static final int MINIMUM_ITERATIONS
      The lowest count a token may carry and still be read.

      The count travels in the token so that the default can be raised without orphaning what is already written. This is the other half of that: a token asking to be read with a derisory count is refused, so the field cannot be edited into a weakness.

      See Also:
      • Constant Field Values

    • MAXIMUM_ITERATIONS

      public static final int MAXIMUM_ITERATIONS
      The highest count a token may carry, which is a bound on damage rather than on cryptography.

      The count is read out of the token and the key is derived from it before GCM can authenticate anything - it has to be, since the derivation is what produces the key the tag is checked with. And because the count is inside the authenticated header, a token whose count was edited can never authenticate: the derivation is then guaranteed to be wasted, and its cost is whatever the edit says.

      Measured, because the shape of the problem is not obvious: PBKDF2 is linear, so 20 million iterations cost 4.2 seconds on JDK 24 and rather more on the Java 8 baseline. Half of all four-byte corruptions are negative and refused instantly by MINIMUM_ITERATIONS; the other half land in the positive range and average around 1.07 billion, which is minutes of CPU inside ConfigFactory.create - an application that looks hung, and then says the value could not be decrypted.

      Ten million is roughly fifty times current guidance, so it is not a limit anybody deriving a key in earnest can reach, and it caps a corrupted file at a few seconds instead of a few minutes.

      See Also:

  • Method Details

    • name

      public String name()
      Description copied from interface: ValueHandler
      The name this handler answers to, which is what appears between ${$ and ::.

      It is the identifier of what the handler does, and the reason there is no registry of numbers here: a second construction arrives as a second name. It is also where a key rotation goes - aes-gcm-2024 registered beside aes-gcm-2025 turns a rotation into an edit to the file, one value at a time.

      A name may not be empty, and may not contain whitespace or any of $ : { }: those are what tell a marker apart from an ordinary key, and a name using them would not be reachable.

      Specified by:
      name in interface ValueHandler
      Returns:
      the name, never null.

    • encrypt

      public String encrypt(String plainText)
      Encrypts a value, producing the token that goes inside a marker. Each call draws a fresh salt and a fresh IV.

      A tool encrypting several values in one run should reuse one salt across them, which is what encryptAll(java.lang.String...) is for: it is the difference between one key derivation and one per value.

      Parameters:
      plainText - the value to encrypt.
      Returns:
      the base64 token.
